big: Rohan's laptop is stolen, then a family member needs a surgery, in the same month. He has no cushion. He borrows on a card at 3% a month. One emergency has now become a long-term debt.

lines: How much should I keep aside, and where do I even put it?
Add up your essential costs for a month and multiply by six. Then keep it where it is safe and reachable in a day.

intro: Only essentials count. Leave out eating out and shopping.
note: Six months is a common target. Single earners or people with unstable income may prefer nine to twelve.

small: ₹20,000 a month for 12 months, in ₹ lakh
alt: Bars growing as the emergency fund builds
caps: ₹20,000 a month goes in on salary day.
Halfway, six months of saving is ₹1.2 lakh, about three months of essentials.
By month twelve, ₹2.4 lakh covers six months of essentials.
It is built slowly. The point is to start and not to stop.

q: Where should an emergency fund be kept?
opts: In equity funds, since they usually grow faster than a savings account
In gold jewellery, since it keeps its value for many years to come
In a savings account or liquid option, safe and reachable in a day
In a five-year fixed deposit, for the highest interest available
why: Equity can be down 20% in the very month you need the money, which defeats the purpose.
Jewellery is slow and costly to sell, so it is not an emergency tool.
The fund has two jobs: stay safe and be reachable within a day. Returns come last.
A long lock-in makes the money hard to reach, and early exit usually carries a penalty.

q: Meena's essentials are ₹30,000 a month. She has ₹1.2 lakh saved. How many months does she have covered?
opts: Four months, since ₹1.2 lakh divided by ₹30,000 is four
Six months, since that is the standard target for everyone
Twelve months, since the fund counts a full year of savings
Two months, since part of it must be kept for non-essentials
why: ₹1,20,000 divided by ₹30,000 gives four months of essentials covered.
Six months is a target. Her actual cover depends on the amount she has saved.
She has covered four months, not a year. The fund is smaller than she may think.
The fund is for essentials only, so the whole amount counts toward them.

q: A phone sale offers 40% off. Rohan wants to use his emergency fund for it. What is the sound choice?
opts: Use it, because a discount of 40% is a rare chance that is worth the money
Use half of it, so that some cushion is left for later
Use it now and refill it within a few years, whenever it is convenient
Leave the fund alone, since a sale is not an emergency
why: A sale is a want. The fund is for real emergencies such as a job loss or a medical bill.
Using half still weakens the cushion for a want. The rule is that it is for emergencies only.
Waiting years to refill leaves a gap when an emergency can strike, so refill promptly.
The fund is for real emergencies only, and a bargain, however good, is not one.

q: Rohan uses ₹80,000 of his fund for a hospital bill. What should he do next?
opts: Nothing, since the fund has done its job and can simply stay lower now
Refill it before other goals, so the cushion is ready again
Switch the whole fund into shares to rebuild it much faster
Stop all other saving until the fund is back to full again
why: A reduced fund leaves him exposed to the next surprise, so it should be rebuilt.
After using it, refill it first. Other goals wait until the cushion is restored.
Shares can fall just when he needs the money, so they are the wrong place for the fund.
Stopping all saving is not needed. Refilling is the priority, and other goals can pause briefly.

pts: Aim for about six months of essential costs.
Keep it safe and reachable within a day. Returns come last.
Use it only for real emergencies, and refill it first after using it.
